prompt: What is the difference between the class `Book` and an object of it?
hint: One is written once; the other is made while the program runs.

choices.text: There is none: `Book` is the object and its fields are the class
choices.why: The fields are part of the description; no book existed until `new Book()` ran.

choices.text: The class describes books; an object is one book made by `new`
choices.why: Right: one class, and as many objects as the program asks for.

choices.text: The class is the `.java` file and the object is the `.class` file
choices.why: The `.class` file is still the description, compiled; objects exist only in a running JVM.

choices.text: An object is a class that has a `main` method
choices.why: `Main` has a `main` and is still a class; objects are made with `new`.

prompt: `first.isbn` was never assigned, and `System.out.println(first.isbn)` printed something. What?
hint: A field always has a value.

choices.text: An empty line, because an unset `String` is `""`
choices.why: The default for a reference is `null`, not the empty string, and `println` printed the word.

choices.text: `null`
choices.why: Right: a reference field nobody assigned holds `null`.

choices.text: Nothing: the program failed to compile, since `isbn` might not have been initialised
choices.why: That error is for local variables; a field gets a default and the program compiled.

choices.text: A `NullPointerException` naming `isbn`
choices.why: Printing `null` is allowed; only reaching through it, as `none.title` did, fails.

prompt: `java Main` printed `Book@251a69d7` for one book. What is that number?
hint: It changes on every run.

choices.text: The object's address in memory
choices.why: The section says it plainly: a hash code, not an address.

choices.text: The ISBN, which was never set and so is random
choices.why: The ISBN printed as `null` on the line above; this number belongs to the object, not a field.

choices.text: A hash code, because `Book` does not say how to describe itself
choices.why: Right: class name, `@`, hash code in hexadecimal; lesson 20 writes a `toString` instead.

choices.text: A running count of the `Book` objects the program has made so far
choices.why: Two books printed two unrelated numbers; nothing counts them.

prompt: `javap -p Book` listed `Book();` although `Book.java` declares only three fields. Where did it come from?
hint: Lesson 1 found the same thing in `Hello`.

choices.text: The compiler wrote a constructor because the class declared none
choices.why: Right: it is what `new Book()` calls, and lesson 13 shows when it disappears.

choices.text: `javap` adds it to every listing, whether or not it is in the file
choices.why: `javap` prints what the class file holds; it invents nothing.

choices.text: It is the `main` method of `Main`, listed under the wrong class
choices.why: `main` belongs to `Main.class`; this is inside `Book.class`.

prompt: Variables declared inside a class and outside any method, such as `title` and `year`, are called ___.
hint: Every object gets its own copy of each.

prompt: A colleague adds a fourth line, `System.out.println(Book.title);`, to `main`. What happens, and why?
hint: Whose title would it be?

choices.text: It prints the title of the last book made
choices.why: The class keeps no record of its objects; there is no "last book" to ask.

choices.text: It prints `null`, the default of a field nobody set
choices.why: There is no field to have a default here: `title` belongs to each object, not to the class.

choices.text: It does not compile: `title` belongs to each object, so it needs an object before the dot
choices.why: Right: every book has its own title, and the class name names none of them; lesson 15 is about fields that do belong to the class.

choices.text: It prints both titles, one per line
choices.why: Nothing in Java loops over a class's objects by itself.

prompt: After `Book b = a;` and `b.title = "Memorial de Aires";`, what does `a.title` read?
hint: How many `new` had run?

choices.text: `Dom Casmurro`, because `b` is a copy of the book
choices.why: The assignment copied the reference, not the book.

choices.text: `Memorial de Aires`
choices.why: Right: `a` and `b` lead to the same object, so a change through one is seen through the other.

choices.text: `null`, because assigning `a` to `b` empties `a`
choices.why: Assignment copies a value into `b` and leaves `a` exactly as it was.

prompt: `a` and `c` are two books whose `title` fields are both `"Memorial de Aires"`. What does `a == c` say?
hint: `==` on references compares one thing.

choices.text: `true`, because every field is equal
choices.why: `==` never looks inside the objects; their contents are irrelevant to it.

choices.text: `true` only if the two titles are the same `String` object
choices.why: The titles do not matter to `a == c`; it compares the two book references.

choices.text: `false`: two `new`, two objects
choices.why: Right: `==` compares identity, and `c` came from its own `new`.

choices.text: It does not compile: `==` is for numbers
choices.why: `==` compiles for references and compares identity; it printed `false`.

prompt: The `NullPointerException` named the variable as `<local4>`. Why not `none`?
hint: The second run used one more flag.

choices.text: `none` is a reserved word, so the JVM may not print it
choices.why: `none` is an ordinary name; with `-g` the message printed it.

choices.text: `javac` keeps no local names unless asked, so the JVM numbers them
choices.why: Right: compiled with `-g`, the same line said `"none" is null`.

choices.text: The JIT compiler renamed the variable while it optimised the method
choices.why: The program never ran long enough to reach the JIT, and the JIT does not rename variables in messages.

choices.text: `null` references lose their names when they are assigned
choices.why: A name belongs to the variable in the source, whatever value it holds.

prompt: In `Refs.main`, the JVM numbers local variables from 0, starting with `args`. Which number does `c` get?
hint: `args`, `a`, `b`, `c`, `none`, in the order they are declared.

prompt: Which of these compare what two `Book` objects contain, rather than whether they are the same object? Choose all that apply.
hint: Asking the objects, or their fields, is a comparison of contents.

choices.text: `a.title.equals(c.title) && a.year == c.year`
choices.why: Yes: the titles compared character by character, and `year` is an `int`, where `==` compares the numbers.
No: that is identity, and it said `false` for two equal books.

choices.text: `a.title == c.title`
choices.why: No: `==` on two `String` references is identity too, as lesson 7 showed.

choices.text: `a.year == c.year`
choices.why: Yes, as far as it goes: `year` is a primitive, so `==` compares the values themselves.

prompt: A method runs `Book b = new Book();`. Where is `b`, and where is the book?
hint: Two regions, kept apart.

choices.text: Both on the stack, in the frame of the method that made them
choices.why: Only locals live in a frame; the book outlives the call whenever a reference still leads to it.

choices.text: `b` in the method's frame on the stack, the book on the heap
choices.why: Right: `b` goes when the call returns, the book stays while something leads to it.

choices.text: Both on the heap, while the stack holds only the bytecode of the method
choices.why: The bytecode is in the class, loaded once; the stack holds frames with their locals.

choices.text: The book in the `.class` file, `b` in memory
choices.why: The `.class` file holds the description; books exist only in a running JVM.

prompt: The histogram showed 1000 `Book` instances taking 24000 bytes. How many bytes is one `Book`?
hint: Divide.

prompt: Put the pieces of one `Book` object in the order the section adds them up to 24 bytes, biggest first.
hint: The header is the largest piece.
items: The 12-byte header that says which class the object is
The two references, `isbn` and `title`, 8 bytes together

prompt: The `[LBook;` line in the histogram is one object of 4016 bytes. What is in it?
hint: Lesson 9 met arrays; this is how the JVM names one.

choices.text: The thousand books themselves, packed side by side
choices.why: Then it would be 24,000 bytes and more; the books are counted on their own line.

choices.text: A header and a thousand references to the books
choices.why: Right: 16 bytes of header and length, then 1000 references of 4 bytes.

choices.text: The class `Shelf`, loaded once
choices.why: A class is not an instance on the heap's histogram line for `[LBook;`; that line counts one array.

choices.text: The thousand `title` strings
choices.why: No title was set in `Shelf`, so no string was made for them.

prompt: `year` is an `int` and `title` is a `String`. What does a `Book` hold for each?
hint: Primitives and references are stored differently.

choices.text: The characters of the `String` title and the year's number, both inside the `Book` object
choices.why: The characters are in a separate object; the book holds the way to it.

choices.text: A reference for each: one to a `String` object and one to an `Integer` object
choices.why: An `int` field holds the number itself; only non-primitive types are references.

choices.text: The number itself for `year`, and for `title` a way to reach the text
choices.why: Right: that is the drawing's second layer, and why `year` costs 4 bytes inside the book.

prompt: `Book x = new Book(); Book y = x; y = new Book(); y.title = "S. Bernardo";` What is `x.title` now?
hint: Follow where `y` leads after each line.

choices.text: `null`
choices.why: Right: `y` was moved to a second book before the title was set, so `x`'s book was never touched.

choices.text: `S. Bernardo`, because `y` was once the same book as `x`
choices.why: It was, until `y = new Book()` gave `y` a different object.

choices.text: Nothing: the second `new` throws because `y` already had a book
choices.why: Assigning a new reference to a variable is always allowed; the old object is simply no longer reached through `y`.

prompt: A program builds a `Book[] shelf = new Book[3];` and immediately prints `shelf[0].title`. What happens?
hint: What does an array of references hold before anything is put in it?

choices.text: It prints `null`, the title's default
choices.why: There is no book whose title could default: the array's slots are `null`, and reaching through one fails.

choices.text: It prints `Book@` and a hash code
choices.why: No `Book` was made; `new Book[3]` makes one array and no books.

choices.text: A `NullPointerException`, because `shelf[0]` is `null`
choices.why: Right: like `Shelf`, the array holds references, and these lead nowhere until `new Book()` fills them.

choices.text: A compile error: the array must be filled before use
choices.why: The compiler does not track what an array holds; the failure comes at run time.

prompt: Match each tool or flag from this lesson to what it showed.
hint: Sections 02, 03 and 04.

pairs.right: The fields and the constructor in the class file
Variable names in an exception's message
The JVMs running for this user
How many objects of each class are on the heap

right_distractors: The hash code of every object

prompt: Which line makes an object?
hint: Only one keyword does it.

choices.text: `Book b = a;`
choices.why: That copies a reference to an object that already exists.

choices.text: `Book none = null;`
choices.why: That declares a variable that leads nowhere.

choices.text: `class Book { String title; }`
choices.why: That describes books; it makes none.

choices.text: `Book c = new Book();`
choices.why: Right: `new` makes the object and the reference to it goes into `c`.
